content.title: Response to Our Reviewers.
content.comment:
Dear Reviewers: 

Thanks for your constructuve comments in such a short reviewing time. The main concern is the novelty of this paper, since partition is widely used in NeRF and some papers have discussed the INR expressive power. Here are our explanations: 1) Most works that utilize partition in NeRF is to mainly improve the inference speed due to the parallel and flexible inference. However, in this paper we focus on the training of pure INRs. We present a theoretical analysis of why partition helps to improve the convergence speed of INR training process, without any effect of differentiable rendering. 2) Some papers about spectral bias have discussed about the expressive power of INRs and find that INR tends to learn lower frequency components first. The boundaries with high gradient are indeed high-frequency components of signals. In this paper, we are the first to present a quantative relation between the convergence speed and the frequency from the point of view of boundaries.  Some other concerns are about our experiments. We will consider adding experiments about the impact of the number of partition heads as well as the performance on various modalities in revised version.

However, considering the over-low scores, we decide to withdraw our work directly. Thank you again for your discussion and suggestions.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of partitioning an image using implicit neural representation with a final goal image segmentation. The paper shows that the  time complexity to force a neural network to fit a discontinuous function is exponentially increasing with the number of high gradients in the input domain, that is called by the authors exponencial-increase hypothesis. Then the authors propose to split the domain in subdomains and apply neural networks on each domain independently. Partition is based on regular grids or hierarchical clustering of superpixels-like regions. Validation is done on 20 test images reporting the PSNR values.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is clearly written and well structured.
2. Motivation is well presented.
3. Mathematical formulation is technically sound.


Weaknesses:
1. My first concern regards the validation: there is no systematic validation following common methodology from the state of the art. The authors say: "We choose a typical landscape image with dimension 380x254". Which is this image and from where is it? Then they choose 20 images from LSUN. Why didn't apply your validation on the whole dataset? What was the criterion to chose these 20 images and not another ones? 
2. There is no comparison to state of the art.
3. The method is based on partition of the image on regular grid. But how do you know that the contour is not crossing the grid? How do you choose the grid resolution? How sensitive is the algorithm on using different grids?
4. In case of hierarchical feature selection based partition, the algorithm presented in the last paragraph of Section 4 contains so many parameters and heuristics so that different partitions can be obtained that definitely will condition the final image segmentation.
5. The hypothesis that more high gradient points there are the higher  the complexity of the fitting of the neural representation is quite obvious.
6. What about situations when a boundary is crossing or is in the interior of another one.
7. Novelty of the learning to learn INR is questionable.
8. Fig.4 should be explained better, what are the rows and the columns?!
9. Image in Fig. 5 is quite easy to segment. Still in this case it is clear that the regular grid method is not working. 
10. The authors are invited to compare their results  and follow the validation methodology of other INR papers like:
Hu, H., Chen, Y., Xu, J., Borse, S., Cai, H., Porikli, F., & Wang, X. (2022). Learning implicit feature alignment function for semantic segmentation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.08655.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written but  the problem is the novelty and the impact for the image segmentation. The techniques are quite simple and thus are easily reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: As mentioned above the novelty, the validation consistency and the impact of the proposed method are not clear.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This submission studies Implicit Neural Representation (INR) for 2D images and observes that estimating a discontinuous function (i.e., natural image) using a continuous function (i.e., neural network) is inefficient. It is argued that the time complexity of the estimation problem is exponential in the number of discontinuities in the natural image.

Given the exponential complexity the authors propose to partition the image (either using a grid or a segmentation) and fit one INR (i.e., network) to each part independently. Thus, complexity is greatly reduced.

The experimental validation shows that the proposed partitioning leads to increased PSNR for fewer optimization steps when learning an INR for a single image, or in the context of meta-learning of INRs for images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

**S1.** The method is motivated and presented with clarity.

**S1.** The method is very simple, yet effective.

## Weaknesses

**W1**. The idea of partitioning a scene and doing estimation within each part independently from others is not novel. In relation to INRs see, e.g., (Tretschk et al. ECCV 2020), (Tancik et al. CVPR 2022) and (Turki et al. CVPR 2022).

**W2.** Hypothesis 1 (namely that the complexity is exponential in the number of boundaries) is simply stated but no insight into its validity for natural images is provided. The rest of the theory merely shows that when hypothesis 1 holds, partitioning benefits efficiency. 

## References

Tretschk et al. PatchNets: Patch-Based Generalizable Deep Implicit 3D Shape Representations. ECCV 2020.

Tancik et al. Block-NeRF: Scalable Large Scene Neural View Synthesis. CVPR 2022.

Turki et al. Mega-NERF: Scalable Construction of Large-Scale NeRFs for Virtual Fly-Throughs. CVPR 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity is good.

Quality and originality are limited. Partitioning has been done many times while the submission does not provide theoretical or empirical insight into how partitioning helps in the 2D image case.
content.summary_of_the_review: The contribution of the submission is very limited. It amounts to the observation that partitioning 2D images (to some extent) is beneficial to the estimation of INRs for 2D images.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper targets an image-fitting problem using implicit neural representations (INRs). The authors argue that an image is piecewise discontinuous, and the time of cost increases with more high-gradient pixels. To solve the issue, the paper proposes to partition the image into sub-regions and fit signals within each region with an independent network. The partition-based method is applied for learning and meta-learning INRs. Experimental results show that the proposed method leads to faster convergence.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:
+ The meta-learning results in Fig. 6 (a) are interesting. It seems that each subregion converges at a similar speed for SIREN_G^G  and SIREN_S^S. Unlike the results in Fig. 6 (a)-SIREN_G and Fig 7, the pixel values around the sub-region boundaries are consistent without artifacts.

Cons:
Though some of the results are interesting, some of the arguments are not solid or not supported by the experiments. The comments are detailed as follows.
1. Piece-wise discontinuity (Page 1, abstract)
The authors claim that images are piece-wise discontinuous, hence they cannot be well recovered by the continuous function parameterized by an INR. However, within each partitioned sub-region, the discontinuity remains, and the locally piece-wise discontinuous signals are still recovered by a single INR. It seems that the proposed partition-based method cannot handle this piece-wise discontinuity issue.
2. Exponential-increase hypothesis (Page 2, introduction)
The empirical finding of exponentially increasing convergence step for high-frequency sinusoids (Fig. 1) leads to the exponential-increase hypothesis. Though the experiment is conducted in a frequency domain, the conclusion is applied in the spatial domain by arguing that more objects (page 1, abstract) or more boundaries (page 3) require a longer training time. This hypothesis is not solid nor well-supported. Firstly, to verify the proposed hypothesis, I would like to see the result that a highly textured image (with more high-gradient pixels) requires more training steps than a common image. On the other hand, the experimental results in Fig. 1 are actually well studied as the SPECTRAL BIAS issue [A, B]: high-frequency components are hard to be learned during training. The expressive power of an INR (including SIREN) is also well studied by [C]: the weights of the MLP actually define the spectral support for the target signal. When it comes to the frequency space, it is hard to say if more boundaries require exponentially-increasing time costs as they may just share similar high-frequency components.
3. INR fails for scaled scenes due to heavy inference time (page 2, related work)
Though this argument is not relevant to the proposed method, the unsatisfactory rendering efficiency issue for the vanilla NeRF mainly contributes to the volume rendering mechanism but not the INR itself, as the integrals along the rendered rays are achieved through sampling, thus requiring multiple forward passes through the INR.
4. Fitting a high-resolution image with a single INR is hard (page 1, introduction)
Though this argument is supported by ACORN (Martel et al., 2021), the experiment is conducted to fit a high-resolution image (mega-pixel resolution for instance). The resolution of 380x254 is applied for learning INRs and the resolution of 256x256 for meta-learning INRs. We don't know if the proposed method can really handle a high-resolution image fitting problem with merely 4 or 9 coarse partitions. 
5. The proposed method achieves better results (experiments)
All results show that the proposed method converges faster at the very beginning (in both learning and meta-learning setups). It is unclear if the proposed method can achieve high PSNR when the networks are trained under more steps till convergence. I would also like to see how a standard SIREN/ReLU MLP would perform at the same size of the model for each sub-region (256/240 units for each layer respectively)

A. Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains, NeurIPS 2020, M Tancik et al.
B. On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks, ICML 2019, N Rahaman et al.
C. A Structured Dictionary Perspective on Implicit Neural Representations, CVPR 2022, G Yüce et al.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new partitioning scheme for learning Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) on Images. This is motivated by the hypothesis that the time complexity of fitting an INR is exponentially increasing with the number of high gradients in the input domain, for which the authors offer a proof. A key contribution is the proposal of a segmentation-based partitioning scheme which utilises existing off-the-shelf algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Moving past a simple grid-based partitioning for INRs is an important research direction, which could have important consequences for scaling INRs to larger dimensional signals. The proposal of a segmentation-approach for images is intuitive and worth studying.
- Section 5.1 shows promising results.

Neural:
- While presented as a major contribution, I find the hypothesis in proof in Section 3.1 neither surprising nor particularly insightful. Other reviewers might feel differently. 

Weaknesses: 
- The authors fail to discuss the generality of their segmentation based partitioning to other modalities. A benefit of the simple grid-style partitioning is that it trivially applies to modalities beyond images (Video, Audio, 3D-Scenes, ...), whereas this would likely require a custom segmentation algorithm for each modality. As those segmentation are likely to vary in quality and complexity, much of the work in assessing the method proposed for a different modality would be left to the reader.
- While initial results in Section 4.1 look promising, the more realistic learning-to-learn scenario (Section 5.2) are significantly weaker, showing that the simple and more general SIREN_G^G outperforms what in my eyes is the key contribution to this work. Table 4 (Appendix) also show the same conclusion. In practice, this leaves the INR community without a significant contribution that would be likely to be used in future work. Unfortunately, the authors provide little insight on why this result is interesting.
- If I understand correctly, there appears to be a lack of discussion of how to handle varying number of segments in each image, instead relying on a fixed number, which is clearly suboptimal (see Figure 4). Indeed in Section 5.1, the authors write "we fix the number of partitioned regions to 4.". How do the authors plan to overcome this issue?
- Quality and clarity lack somewhat. 

Suggestion:
- The segmentation-based approach could be interesting in image (and video) compression with INRs [1][2]. This is due to the compression memory and runtime cost that is paid for each partition. An intelligent reduction in the size of the number of partitions based on segmentation could show promising results on a rate-distortion plot.
- Grid-based partitioning can sometimes lead to grid artefacts (see qualitative examples in [1] ) which I would expect to be less severe or noticeable when good segmentation is employed. Can the authors check whether this is indeed the case?
- A better analysis of the architectural benefits of the head-based technique (Section 3.3) in comparison to e.g. separate Modulations for each partition [3] would be interesting. A discussion of memory requirements of the MAML training phase for large images with either POG or POS would also be interesting. 

[1] Dupont, Emilien, et al. "Coin++: Data agnostic neural compression." arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.12904 (2022).

[2] Schwarz, Jonathan Richard, and Yee Whye Teh. "Meta-Learning Sparse Compression Networks." arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.08957 (2022).

[3] Dupont, Emilien, et al. "From data to functa: Your data point is a function and you should treat it like one." arXiv preprint arXiv:2201.122
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity & Quality:
- While the manuscript is mostly clear, I have some concerns about a lack of focus and presentation:
     - Table 1 features a column "#hidden layers/head" which I'm unsure about. Naively this would read as the number of hidden layers per head, which seems like an oxymoron. Is it the number of hidden units used in the torso of the network to ensure comparable #Total Param.?
    - Table 3 and Figure 6: It's not clear to me why the evaluation setup of training/testing on different partitioning strategies is shown in so much detail. What would be a practical advantage of doing so? P_G^G and P_S^S clearly see like the better options. This distracts from the key message.
    - I'm unsure about why ReLU MLPs with positional embeddings feature so heavily in the experimental section given that they seem a significantly less attractive choice. Moving this comparison in the Appendix would open room for a more detailed discussion of the segmentation idea.
    - Equation (8). What is F(x_i)? F seems to be defined of a set of networks, not a function (Earlier in the same paragraph).
    - Grammar and vocabulary could be refined to improve presentation. Phrases like "pretty hard" is somewhat colloquial. Articles are sometimes missing, e.g. "we apply Adam optimizer" -> "we apply the Adam optimizer"

Reproducibility:
- No concerns regarding reproducibility
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall an interesting idea that deserves investigation and could have interesting results for e.g. compression with INRs. Unfortunately, the authors do not present a method that appears to show sufficient practical improvements despite the limited domain (Images only). In addition, the lack of discussion around the generality of the technique for other modalities as well as other unaddressed questions (Varying number of segments per image) makes this currently unsuitable for publication. I have however provided several technical suggestions that could help explore the idea in more depth.

content.title: Partition Matters in Learning and Learning-to-Learn Implicit Neural Representations
content.abstract: $\textit{Implicit neural representation}$ (INR) aims to learn a $\textit{continuous function}$ (i.e., a neural network) to represent an image, where the input and output of the function are pixel coordinator and RGB/Gray values, respectively. However, images tend to consist of many objects whose colors are not perfectly consistent, resulting in the challenge that image itself is actually a $\textit{discontinuous piecewise function}$ and cannot be well estimated by a continuous function. In this paper, we empirically investigate that if a neural network is enforced to fit a discontinuous piecewise function (e.g., a step function) to reach a fixed small error $\epsilon$, the time costs will increase exponentially. We name this phenomenon as $\textit{exponential-increase}$ hypothesis. Obviously, handling an image with many objects is almost impossible in INR if this hypothesis is true. To address this issue, we first prove that partitioning a complex signal into several sub-regions and utilizing piecewise INRs to fit that signal can significantly reduce the convergence time, even when the exponential-increase hypothesis is true. Based on this fact, we introduce two partition-based INR methods: one for learning INRs, and the other for learning-to-learn INRs. Both methods are designed to partition an image into different sub-regions, and dedicate smaller networks for each part. In addition, we further propose two partition rules based on regular grids and semantic segmentation maps, respectively. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed partitioning methods in terms of learning INR for a single image (ordinary learning framework) and the learning-to-learn framework.
